In Washington, the Senate passed a permitting overhaul 62-33 and blocked a resolution to end hostilities with Iran, while the White House replaced its national cyber director after a wave of tech outages. stories.headline: White House replaces national cyber director after a week of tech outages
stories.summary: Sean Cairncross is out as White House national cyber director, days after outages disrupted air travel, banking and government systems. stories.why_it_matters: The office coordinates federal cybersecurity policy, and the change comes while travelers, bank customers and federal agencies are still dealing with a run of outages whose causes have not been fully explained.
stories.background: The national cyber director advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates policy across federal agencies. Over the past week, outages hit Microsoft services, flights, banks and a National Security Agency network. stories.headline: Senate passes bipartisan permitting overhaul 62-33, sending it to the House
stories.summary: The Senate voted 62-33 Thursday night for a bill that would speed federal permitting reviews for energy and infrastructure projects and limit legal challenges to them. Thirty-one Democrats and two Republicans voted no. The bill now needs House approval before going to President Trump.

stories.headline: Senate Republicans block a resolution to end the Iran war in first vote since the midterms
stories.summary: Senate Republicans on Thursday blocked a war powers resolution that would have directed President Trump to end hostilities with Iran. Democrats and a small number of Republicans supported it. Democrats, who are set to take control of both chambers, have not settled on a plan for what they will do next.

stories.headline: Justice Department moves to drop its lawsuit over Alaska's Senate race after Peltola's win
stories.summary: The Justice Department asked a federal appeals court Thursday to dismiss the lawsuit it filed before the election seeking to block certification of Alaska's US Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan lost. Democrat Mary Peltola won the race this week.

stories.headline: Trump's nominee to lead CISA declines to say who won in 2020 or call Jan. 6 an attack
stories.summary: Michael LoSapio, nominated to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, told senators Thursday he does not consider the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot an "attack" and would not say who won the 2020 presidential election. stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin end first three-way summit with a nuclear-risk pledge and no Ukraine deal
stories.summary: The presidents of the United States, China and Russia met together for the first time on Thursday in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Trump had proposed that such a meeting focus on nuclear weapons. It took place while Russia's war in Ukraine continues, with Russian strikes hitting Kyiv during and after the summit. Trump and Putin had last met in Alaska in August 2025.

stories.headline: Russian missiles damage Kyiv bridges after Ukraine's strikes on the Crimea bridge; missiles fall in Poland
stories.summary: Russia fired missiles and drones at Kyiv overnight into Friday, damaging bridges over the Dnipro River, cutting power and killing several people. The attack followed three Ukrainian strikes in four days on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, after which Vladimir Putin promised retaliation. Poland said Russian missiles and a drone came down on its territory during the attack.
stories.why_it_matters: The exchange hit transport links that civilians rely on in a capital city, and weapons landed inside a NATO member. Putin also said he would not negotiate a limited ceasefire now, which lowers the chances of an early pause in the fighting.
stories.background: Russia and Ukraine are at war, and Russia holds the Crimean peninsula, which it annexed from Ukraine. The Kerch Bridge links Russia to Crimea, carries rail traffic that Reuters says matters to Russian logistics, and is described by outlets as a symbol of Putin's rule there. This week's Ukrainian strikes halted rail traffic on the bridge. At the same time, U.S. envoys, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders met in Berlin to discuss terms for ending the war, and Putin met the U.S. and Chinese presidents in Shenzhen.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said new talks on Ukraine that include European leaders could be held soon on neutral ground, and Putin said Russia had invited European representatives to Moscow.

stories.headline: Myanmar rejects UN court's genocide ruling as Rohingya refugees ask when they can go home
stories.summary: A day after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, Myanmar called the decision unfair. Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh welcomed the ruling and said they want to return home, and rights groups called for sanctions. Malaysia said it plans to resettle 10,000 Rohingya in Turkey.
stories.why_it_matters: More than a million people remain in refugee camps with no date for return, and the court has no force of its own to change that. Only left-leaning and center outlets in the digest covered the ruling; no right-leaning outlet did.
stories.background: The Rohingya are a Muslim minority from Myanmar. A military campaign in 2017 drove hundreds of thousands of them out of the country, most into neighboring Bangladesh. Gambia brought a case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' top court, under the 1948 Genocide Convention; the court ordered protective measures in 2020 and allowed the case to proceed in 2022. Myanmar has denied genocide and has described its actions as counter-terrorism. The court ruled on Thursday, Nov. 19.

stories.summary: Saudi Arabia said a Houthi attack on Thursday damaged several floors of the tallest building in Riyadh, which houses the Public Investment Fund, and that no one was hurt. stories.headline: New draft deal at UN climate talks removes all mention of fossil fuels on the final day
stories.summary: A new draft agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, no longer mentions fossil fuels. Australia, which is leading the negotiations, released the text on Thursday, and nearly 200 countries were due to finish on Friday. Campaign groups objected, and outlets differ on how close a deal is.
stories.why_it_matters: These agreements shape how fast governments move away from coal, oil and gas, which affects energy bills, jobs and the pace of warming. Only center outlets and wire services in the digest covered the draft.
stories.background: COP is the annual United Nations climate conference where nearly 200 countries negotiate joint commitments. This year's meeting, COP31, is hosted by Turkey in Antalya, with Australia running the negotiations. The future of coal, oil and gas has been the most contested question. An earlier draft released on Nov. 16 called for faster action to phase out fossil fuels, and oil-producing countries have long resisted such wording.

facts.text: The draft that Australia released on Thursday drops any mention of fossil fuels.
The draft also removes dates for reaching net zero and an earlier demand to phase out unilateral trade measures such as the European Union's carbon border tax by 2027, The Hindu reported.
Campaign groups reacted with anger to the new text, France 24 reported.
Nearly 200 countries had until Friday to reach a deal.
The Financial Times reported that the talks have turned toward carbon capture and that critics say the final sessions focus on energy security.
The earlier draft, published Nov. 16, called for "accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels", according to Daily Sabah.

stories.headline: UK and EU meet in Brussels to agree food trade, carbon and youth mobility deals
stories.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham met European Union leaders Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa in Brussels on Friday for a summit meant to rebuild ties after Brexit. The two sides were expected to announce deals on food trade, carbon emissions and a scheme letting young people live and work across each other's borders.

stories.background: Britain voted to leave the European Union a decade ago, and its departure added checks on trade and limits on living and working across the border. A first UK-EU summit in 2025 began a process both sides call a reset. Andy Burnham, now prime minister, has said he hopes to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime and argues closer ties will help the economy. The EU side is led by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

stories.headline: Somalia orders the UAE ambassador to leave within 72 hours

stories.headline: Stocks extend their losing streak worldwide as the AI sell-off deepens
stories.summary: U.S. stocks fell sharply again on Thursday, with the Dow down about 1,100 points and the Nasdaq off 2.3%, as investors kept selling companies tied to artificial intelligence. The selling spread to Asia and Europe on Friday, and U.S. futures pointed lower before the open. Anthropic's record stock-market debut on Thursday did not reverse the trend.
stories.why_it_matters: Most retirement accounts and index funds hold large positions in the technology companies being sold, so a long slide in AI shares shows up directly in 401(k) and savings balances. Next week's Black Friday sales figures will be watched as a check on whether consumer spending is holding up.
stories.background: Much of the stock market's gain in recent years has come from companies building or supplying artificial intelligence, such as chipmakers and big technology firms that are spending heavily on data centers. Investors have recently grown more doubtful that this spending will pay off, and the sector was shaken further when Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang left the company amid a scandal. Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, went public on Thursday in the largest initial public offering on record, and some investors had hoped strong demand for its shares would restore confidence in the sector. Instead the wider market kept falling, and the losses spread overseas.

stories.summary: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday after raising about $81 billion, the most ever raised in an initial public offering. Its shares closed around $97, 17% above the $83 offer price, after opening at $111.50. Bloomberg reported the stock was down more than 6% early Friday.
stories.why_it_matters: The listing lets ordinary investors buy into a major AI developer for the first time, and many did, but analysts quoted by CNBC warn the shares are likely to swing widely in the coming weeks. The stock's early moves are also being read as a signal for the wider AI sector that many index funds hold.
stories.background: Anthropic is an artificial intelligence company led by chief executive Dario Amodei and best known for its Claude chatbot. It is the first of the major AI labs to sell shares to the public; until now only private investors could own a stake. In an initial public offering, a company sells shares at a set price and they then trade freely on an exchange, where the price can rise or fall. The deal came during a broad sell-off in AI-linked stocks and passed the previous record set by SpaceX in June.

stories.headline: Walmart raises its sales outlook again but warns fuel costs are squeezing prices
stories.summary: Walmart raised its full-year outlook for the third time after what the Associated Press called a solid quarter, helped by online sales and by higher-income shoppers looking for deals. The company also said higher diesel and transportation costs are making it harder to hold prices down. The results come a week before Black Friday.
stories.why_it_matters: Walmart serves a large share of U.S. households, so its results are a read on how households are coping with high prices. Its warning on fuel costs suggests pressure on shelf prices may continue through the holidays.
stories.background: Walmart reports its sales and profit every three months and gives a forecast for the full year, which investors treat as a gauge of consumer spending. Retailers including Walmart and Target say shoppers are focused on saving money amid worries about the economy. Fuel prices have been high this year, raising the cost of trucking goods to stores. The company's report came just before the holiday shopping season, the most important sales period for retailers.

stories.summary: Members of Congress released figures showing the Commerce Department approved sales of more than 800,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, some of which the New York Times reported have military ties. stories.headline: Mamdani sets end of 2032 as new target for closing Rikers Island
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani released a plan Friday to end incarceration on Rikers Island by the end of 2032, more than five years after the deadline now written into city law. The plan would move the remaining jail population to smaller facilities in four boroughs and depends on cutting the number of people held. The City Council has to approve the new deadline.
stories.why_it_matters: The plan decides where and how the city holds people awaiting trial, how much it spends to shrink the jail population, and when four new borough jails open in residential neighborhoods. Most of the coverage in today's digest comes from left-leaning and center outlets.
stories.background: Rikers Island is New York City's main jail complex, and it has a long record of assaults and deaths among people held there. A city law passed in 2019 requires the complex to shut by Aug. 31, 2027, and to be replaced by four smaller jails in the boroughs. Those jails are under construction and are not expected to be finished until 2032, and Council members have been working on a bill to push the legal deadline back. Mamdani said during his campaign that he would work toward the 2027 date; his administration now says the city will miss it. Any new date needs a vote of the City Council.

stories.headline: Building next to deadly Flatbush collapse to be demolished; MTA bus video shows the moment it fell
stories.summary: City officials said Wednesday that 1323 Flatbush Ave., the apartment building next to the one that collapsed last week and killed eight people, must be torn down. The collapse tore the side wall off the adjoining building at 1323 Flatbush Ave. The Department of Buildings, the city agency that issues construction permits and inspects sites, is investigating.

stories.headline: Mamdani signs carriage horse ban; drivers' union sues within minutes
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Thursday signed a law that winds down the city's horse-drawn carriage industry by June 2028. Transport Workers Union Local 100, which represents the drivers, filed a lawsuit to stop it shortly after the signing. Former Mayor Bill de Blasio tried to ban it and failed. markets.summary: U.S. stocks dropped on Thursday: the Dow fell about 1,100 points, or 2.2%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 2.3%, and the S&P 500 fell again, extending what the Associated Press called Wall Street's longest losing streak since 2024. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, raised a record $81 billion and its shares rose 17% on their first day, but the debut did not stop investors from selling other stocks tied to artificial intelligence amid doubts about how much AI companies are worth. The selling carried into Friday, with Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, European technology shares falling and U.S. stock futures (bets on where indexes will open) pointing lower; Bloomberg reported Anthropic's own shares gave back more than 6% in early trading. Reuters reported that Wall Street's "fear gauge", a measure of how big investors expect stock swings to be, touched a seven-month high. The average 30-year mortgage rate rose to 7.28%.

concept.explanation: The VIX, often called Wall Street's "fear gauge", is a number that shows how much investors expect the S&P 500 to swing over the next 30 days. It is calculated from the prices of options, which are contracts investors buy to protect themselves against big moves; when more people pay up for that protection, the VIX rises. It usually jumps when stocks fall fast and sinks when markets are calm. It doesn't change your bills directly, but a high reading means the stock funds in a retirement account are likely to move more from day to day, and long stretches of market fear can make companies slower to hire and invest.
